fatal_errors: The proposed Ag surface coating does not reconstruct the target intervention, which was varying Mo content in an SPS-fabricated CoCrFeNiMox-Ni/MoS2-Ag-Cr2O3 bulk composite.
The assumed laser-printed, coarse-grained, unmodified CoCrFeNi starting material is inconsistent with the powder-mixed and sintered composite baseline.
The proposed 10–100 mN load range is orders of magnitude below the target 8 N condition, and the counterface, sliding speed, distance, and temperature test points are not specified.

The cited evidence concerns a bulk TiNbZr-Ag alloy and a wear-induced oxide nanocomposite under different conditions; it does not validate an Ag coating on CoCrFeNi or durable lubrication from room temperature through 800 °C.
The hypothesis assumes that Ag alone remains intact and lubricating throughout the full range without addressing coating depletion, thermal softening, or the intermediate-temperature wear maximum.
explanation: The response addresses the broad challenge and offers a testable surface-engineering alternative, but it misses the target material system, intervention, baseline, and test conditions. There is limited mechanistic overlap because Ag can lower interfacial shear, yet the target behavior depends jointly on Mo-induced lattice distortion and sigma-phase strengthening, low-temperature MoS2/Ag lubrication, and high-temperature NiO/silver-molybdate glaze formation. The predicted uniformly improved behavior also omits the experimentally important friction peak near 200 °C and wear peak near 400 °C. The paired coated-versus-uncoated experiment is directionally useful, but needs fixed coating thickness, adhesion characterization, an 8 N Si3N4 ball-on-disk protocol, specified speed and distance, replicate statistics, and temperature-resolved chemical analysis. Most importantly, the supplied evidence cannot support extrapolation from a bulk TiNbZr-Ag reactive nanocomposite to an Ag-coated CoCrFeNi surface across 25–800 °C.
